title: Don’t Fall for a Simple Story
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane previews Emily Hanford's second season of Sold a Story, which will cover math and Direct Instruction, and warns against the simple narrative that inquiry curricula caused US achievement to collapse and that returning to just telling students will fix it. He agrees that curriculum adoption has shifted toward inquiry and that he dislikes curricula like Illustrative Mathematics because exploration crowds out practice and overloads struggling students. But he points out that PISA shows declines across most countries, so US curriculum choices cannot be the whole explanation. He then describes what Direct Instruction actually looks like: constant choral responses, carefully designed examples and non-examples, heavy cumulative review, mastery-based placement and tested scripts. His conclusion is that teachers can learn a great deal from Engelmann but only by moving past caricatures of both approaches.
points: US adoption of inquiry-focused math curricula has genuinely grown, but the evidence does not show that it caused the decline in achievement.
PISA declines across most developed countries suggest larger forces such as social media and phones, and the US actually improved its relative standing.
Real Direct Instruction is not lecture: it is rapid, response-heavy, built on example sequences, cumulative review and mastery placement.
Kane's own practice combines strong curricula with more explicit teaching and extra practice, which he sees as the realistic path.
quotes: My basic take is that so much time is spent exploring and discussing that practice gets crowded out. While explorations can work for some students, the cognitive load is often high enough that struggling students don’t know what’s going on and check out entirely.
Adopting a curriculum and changing teaching practice are two different things.
That’s not consistent with curriculum change in the US: Illustrative Mathematics did not cause plummeting achievement across the developed world.
Students are constantly answering questions. It’s rare in a DI lesson for a student to go more than a minute or two without answering a question, often via choral response.
Explanations play a relatively small role. Instead, DI uses carefully-designed sequences of examples and non-examples to help students understand new ideas.
Students move on when they master material. The curriculum doesn’t keep going because of a pacing guide.
But the simple story, that inquiry-based curriculum is bad and if we just booted them learning would skyrocket, isn’t consistent with the data.
